figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: EarthJev framework. (a) All 12 bands of a Sentinel-2 patch enter the vision encoder of Qwen3.5-0.8B through a widened input layer, the only trained part of the encoder. Each typed question declares its options; in one forward pass the model returns a probability for every option of every question, and no other model’s output enters its input. The probabilities are the outputs of the released model on a test patch (two most probable options): the first and third answers are right; urban fabric covers 11% of the patch, so the second answer is wrong, with a probability close to 0.5. (b) The answer is read from the logits of the option letters at the last position, so no token is generated; the model is trained with cross-entropy plus Brier score on these letters, and one temperature per question type is fitted on validation.
figures.headline: One forward pass returns a probability for every option of each question, and the wrong urban-fabric answer gets a probability close to 0.5.
citing_sentences: EarthJev, a 0.8B-parameter model that answers typed natural-language questions about Sentinel-2 patches from all 12 bands, with a probability for every option and without generating text (Figure 1).

abstract: Vision-language models for remote sensing answer questions about satellite images by generating text: every answer costs a decoding loop, has to be parsed back to an option, and comes without a usable probability. We present EarthJev, a 0.8B-parameter model that answers typed questions about multispectral Sentinel-2 patches without generating any token. All 12 bands enter the vision encoder of Qwen3.5-0.8B through a widened input layer initialised from the RGB kernels, and, following the open OneJev recipe, the answer is read from the logits of the option letters at a single position and trained with cross-entropy plus Brier score. Under a pre-specified analysis plan, we compare it with the same backbone fine-tuned to generate the answer and with three multimodal language models fine-tuned with LoRA, all trained on the same 70,890 questions from 5% of BigEarthNet v2.0 and timed in one job on the same GPU; VQA models that classify over a fixed answer vocabulary are reported as a reference for the cost of answering only the questions seen in training. EarthJev answers a question in 19.9 ms, 4.3 to 8.7 times faster than the multimodal language models and 6.8 times faster than its own backbone used generatively; when all the questions about an image are asked together, it answers them in 42.8 ms, 3.7 to 10.1 times faster than the batched generative models. On 36,028 test questions it reaches 86.0% accuracy (three seeds), 0.6 and 1.2 points below the two 2B multimodal models and 3.5 points below the remote-sensing EarthDial-4B, with answers that are valid by construction and calibrated probabilities (ECE 0.006). Replacing the nine non-RGB bands with their mean costs 4.5 points, so the model uses the multispectral input, and in an ablation training the whole vision encoder raises accuracy to 88.4% at the same cost. Code and model: https://github.com/CosmoIknosLab/EarthJev.

sections.body: Answering a satellite-image question with generated text costs a decoding loop, needs parsing back to an option, and gives no probability. EarthJev reads the answer from the logits of the option letters at one position, so no token is generated. All 12 Sentinel-2 bands enter a widened input layer of Qwen3.5-0.8B. On 36,028 test questions, it is 4.3 to 8.7 times faster per question than multimodal language models and 6.8 times faster than its own backbone used generatively. Its accuracy is 0.6–1.2 points below the two 2B models. Replacing the nine non-RGB bands with their mean costs 4.5 points. The model is not as accurate as the 4B remote-sensing model, and its frozen vision encoder is the main limit.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Generated answers to satellite-image questions cost decoding time, need parsing, and give no probability.

sections.body: Remote-sensing VQA models classify over a fixed answer vocabulary and do not accept arbitrary option sets. Remote-sensing vision-language models, including EarthDial, answer in free text. The TypeSafe System One interface returns typed probabilities, and OneJev implements a multimodal version trained with cross-entropy plus Brier loss. OneJev's training data contain no remote-sensing source. RSJEV, developed concurrently, uses a one-pass module for RGB scene classification. EarthJev differs in task, input and calibration evaluation. The Brier score and log-loss are strictly proper scoring rules, which is why OneJev, and therefore EarthJev, trains on both.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Prior work either classifies over fixed answer sets or generates free text, and one-pass decision models lack multispectral data.

sections.body: A request gives a state and typed questions, and the model returns probabilities without generating text. A choice question with at most 255 named options returns a distribution over its options and a confidence. The logits of the option letters at the last input position are divided by a temperature fitted per question type and option count on validation data, then passed through a softmax. The first convolution of the vision encoder is widened from 3 to 12 channels. The red, green and blue kernels are copied to B04, B03 and B02, and the other nine start at zero, so before training the logits match the RGB model's on 256 test questions. Only the widened input layer is trained, at learning rate 5×10^-6, and the rest of the encoder stays frozen.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: The answer is read from option-letter logits at one position, and the input layer is widened from three to twelve channels.

sections.body: The study uses 24,000 patches, a 5% subset of BigEarthNet v2.0 stratified by split and country. The questions are 70,890 for training, 36,698 for validation and 36,028 for test, in five types. Every answer is computed from the reference mask, and cases near a decision boundary are skipped. Test questions are written twice, once with seen templates and once with unseen templates, to measure generalisation to new phrasings. Two external benchmarks are used only for transfer: 29,501 presence questions from RSVQAxBEN on 1,437 images, and BigEarthNet.txt with 6,927 binary and 5,550 multiple-choice questions. Answering from the masks with the same rules gives 100% accuracy, which checks the generator.
sections.heading: Data and benchmarks
sections.headline: Questions are generated from reference land-cover masks on a 5% subset of BigEarthNet v2.0, with held-out templates for testing.

sections.body: Tables 1 and 2 compare speed and quality. EarthJev reaches 86.0±0.1% accuracy on the CORINE test set with ECE 0.006. It answers in 19.9 ms per question at batch 1, against 84.5 ms to 171.8 ms for the multimodal models. With all questions of an image asked together, it takes 42.8 ms, while the generative models take 157.3 ms to 431.6 ms. The same backbone fine-tuned to generate reaches 86.8±0.2%. The ResNet-50 fixed-vocabulary model is more accurate at 87.5±0.2% and faster at 12.1 ms, but it answers only trained questions. In an ablation with one seed, training the whole vision encoder raises CORINE accuracy to 88.4%.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: EarthJev is 4.3 to 8.7 times faster per question than multimodal models, with 86.0% accuracy on 36,028 test questions.

sections.body: EarthJev answers only questions with declared options, so user questions must first be mapped to typed questions. Its accuracy is 0.6–1.2 points below the 2B multimodal models and 3.5 points below EarthDial-4B. The pre-specified equivalence and superiority hypotheses are therefore not supported. The 2.5-point gain from training the whole encoder comes from one seed. Latency depends on software: the generative baselines ran without an optimised serving engine, and varied by up to 26% between jobs. The multimodal models see only a three-channel composite, so part of the accuracy gap may come from the input. Calibration outside the training regions and seasons is untested, and EarthDial may have seen test images.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Closed answers, lower accuracy than the 2B and 4B models, and the frozen vision encoder limit what the results support.

sections.body: EarthJev uses the extra bands. Reading answers at one position gives answers that are valid by construction, with probabilities that need no decoding. It is 6.8 times faster than the same backbone used generatively, and 4.3 to 8.7 times faster than multimodal models 2.6 to 5 times larger. Per question it takes 1.2–1.6 times as long as the fixed-vocabulary VQA models, while accepting any declared option set. The stated next steps are training the vision encoder and larger backbones under a pre-specified plan, training on all of BigEarthNet v2.0, and testing outside the training distribution. Code and model are released.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Reading option letters at one position is fast and calibrated; the frozen vision encoder is the main limit to address next.

sections.body: The state is the same for every patch. It describes the sensor and contains nothing derived from the image, and the image placeholder is replaced by the 64 visual tokens of the 12-band patch. RGB-only models receive the same state, with the sensor described as a true-colour composite (B4, B3, B2). Table 5 lists the templates for dominant, presence, share, location and compare questions. Each type has seen templates, used for training and the main test set, and one unseen template, used only for the second rendering of the test set.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix gives the serialised example state and the question templates, with one unseen template per question type.
